title: Shoosmiths offers £1 million bonus pot to encourage AI use among staff (Legal Cheek article + anonymous comment thread)
pub: Legal Cheek (news item with practitioner comment thread beneath)
author: Angus Simpson; anonymous Legal Cheek commenters

dom.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source describes contrasting institutional approaches to AI adoption and raises a narrow concern that prompt-volume incentives may not measure useful activity. This is compatible with the cluster’s warning that access and usage statistics do not establish successful workflow transformation, but it does not assess bounded productivity gains, verification, competence risks or supervised workflow redesign sufficiently to take a clear position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: But Shoosmiths strategy with integrating AI — not least with monetary rewards for using it – also diverges from other firms’ more cautious approaches.
After all, nobody said the million prompts had to be useful in any material sense.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source accepts that AI can complement lawyers by reducing mundane administrative work, while materially extending the cluster’s governance point through a concrete adoption-incentive problem: prompt-count rewards may measure activity rather than productive workflow outcomes and invite gaming. Its productivity and career claims remain anonymous predictions, not evidence of staffing effects.
qs: After all, nobody said the million prompts had to be useful in any material sense.
Your colleagues who learn to use AI will be much more productive as they reduce the time spent on mundane administrative tasks.

kp.k: Shoosmiths ties additional staff bonuses to AI prompt volume
kp.d: Angus Simpson's 2 April 2025 article reports that Shoosmiths is the first major UK law firm to announce bonuses linked to AI use. One million Microsoft Copilot prompts would unlock an extra £1 million for the collegiate bonus pot. Partners and business services directors are excluded from the payout but encouraged to use the technology. The firm says four prompts per employee per working day would readily achieve the target; the article reports an announced scheme, not achievement of the target.
qs: If — or when — the one million prompt target is hit, Shoosmiths will “unlock” an extra £1 million for the collegiate bonus pot.
All staff, except partners and business services directors (who are nevertheless encouraged to use the technology), will benefit.
According to the firm, if each employee used Copilot just four times per working day, the target would be easily reached.

kp.k: Firm frames AI as augmentation rather than staff replacement
kp.d: CEO David Jackson links the initiative to innovation and client benefits. Shoosmiths hopes AI will release lawyers' time for problem-solving, trust-building and supporting clients, while stating that AI will not replace staff. These are the firm's expectations and assurances, rather than demonstrated productivity or employment outcomes.
qs: “We don’t fear AI”, said Shoosmiths CEO David Jackson
Shoosmiths hopes the initiative “frees” lawyers’ time to do “the human-to-human work that really matters: solving problems, building trust, and supporting clients through complexity.”
The statement added that AI “won’t replace” any staff.

kp.k: Adoption includes training, knowledge sharing and new internal roles
kp.d: The article reports a Microsoft partnership supporting training and firmwide sharing of AI use cases, alongside newly launched innovation and data roles. The stated objective is to embed AI in everyday work for both lawyers and support staff.
qs: Shoosmiths’ initiative is backed by a partnership with Microsoft, which includes training and a firmwide “knowledge hub” where teams will share AI use cases and success stories.
New internal roles – including “innovation leads” under a “head of legal innovation” plus a “data manager” – have also been launched.
The move to offer a financial reward for using AI signals Shoosmiths’ commitment to “embedding AI into the day-to-day work” for lawyers and support staff.

kp.k: Shoosmiths links AI adoption to its sustainability ambition
kp.d: The firm claims AI use will help achieve its net zero goals by 2040, while acknowledging upstream AI emissions must be managed. The document presents this as a firm claim without measured environmental results.
qs: The firm also claims AI usage will help them achieve their net zero goals by 2040.
This will mean managing “upstream emissions from AI” in approaching sustainability.

kp.k: Legal employers take divergent approaches to AI adoption
kp.d: The article contrasts Shoosmiths' incentives with Hill Dickinson's restrictions following increased use. It reports A&O Shearman and Macfarlanes adopting Harvey, and different approaches to recruitment applications: Shoosmiths advises using AI to refine original thinking, A&O Shearman issued guidance, and prospective barristers were barred from generative AI use in pupillage applications that year. These are reported institutional practices, not evidence of comparative effectiveness.
qs: Shoosmiths described AI use as “tool to refine and develop your own original thoughts, not replace them”
But Shoosmiths strategy with integrating AI — not least with monetary rewards for using it – also diverges from other firms’ more cautious approaches.

kp.k: Commenters question whether prompt counts reward useful work
kp.d: An anonymous self-described Shoosmiths associate jokes that irrelevant recipe prompts could earn the bonus; another commenter characterises the scheme as reputation-building and predicts arbitrary prompting to protect bonuses. A third proposes automated numerical prompting, while a later commenter tentatively disputes Copilot's ability to execute it. These are anonymous criticisms and hypothetical gaming scenarios, not evidence of actual misuse.
qs: After all, nobody said the million prompts had to be useful in any material sense.
cue associates putting random bs into copilot to make sure they’re not shafted in bonus season for no good reason

Take the current number as input, increment it by 1, and use the result as the next prompt. Begin with 1 and continue this process until reaching 1,000,000. Each number should be considered a new prompt.
Copilot does not have the ability to do recursive or serialised prompting in this manner, I think.

kp.k: Commenters favour legal-specific capability over generalist Copilot incentives
kp.d: One anonymous commenter suggests investing attention in Harvey or a Shoosmiths-developed system rather than generalist Copilot, arguing this could better build legal-tech capability for staff and clients. Another suggests spending £1 million on a functioning platform. These are recommendations and expressions of dissatisfaction, unsupported by comparative tool-performance evidence in the document.
qs: Interesting move but I wonder if the focus should be on a legal specific AI like Harvey or a Shoosmiths-developed tool, rather than a generalist system like Copilot.
Feels like a missed opportunity to build real legal-tech capability for the staff and clients.
Alternatively, consider spending 1 million quid on an AI platform that actually works ya jabronis

kp.k: Self-described partner predicts competitive disadvantages for AI-resistant lawyers
kp.d: An anonymous self-described partner's 18 April 2025 comment predicts that colleagues learning AI will become more productive by reducing mundane administrative work and warns that resistance could threaten continued employment. This is an individual commenter's prediction, not Shoosmiths policy or measured labour-market evidence.
qs: Keep that attitude and you will not be around for long.
Your colleagues who learn to use AI will be much more productive as they reduce the time spent on mundane administrative tasks.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Simpson reports that Shoosmiths is using a collective financial incentive to embed AI in everyday work.
pts.d: The article describes Shoosmiths as the first major UK law firm to announce usage-linked bonuses. The reported scheme unlocks an additional £1 million collective bonus pot when staff reach one million Microsoft Copilot prompts; this is a usage target, not a reported measure of productivity or work quality. The firm estimates that four uses per employee per working day would suffice. Simpson also reports training, knowledge sharing and new innovation and data roles.

pts.k: Shoosmiths predicts that AI will free lawyers for client-facing human work without replacing staff.
pts.d: CEO David Jackson presents AI adoption as a source of client benefits. The firm's statement frames AI as augmentation: freeing time for problem-solving, trust-building and helping clients navigate complexity. Its assurance that staff will not be replaced is a stated commitment or prediction, not an observed employment outcome.

pts.k: Shoosmiths claims AI use will contribute to its sustainability objectives.
pts.d: The firm links AI adoption to achieving net zero by 2040, while acknowledging the need to manage upstream AI emissions. The article supplies no quantified emissions impact or detailed mechanism.

pts.k: Simpson describes uneven adoption across the profession, with encouragement coexisting with restrictions.
pts.d: The article cites A&O Shearman and Macfarlanes adopting Harvey, a legal-AI product, while contrasting Shoosmiths' incentive scheme with Hill Dickinson's restrictions after increased usage and a prohibition on generative AI in pupillage applications. Simpson also references earlier Legal Cheek reporting that over 70% of lawyers regarded AI as a force for good and over 40% used it. These are reported adoption and attitude claims, not findings about improved legal outcomes.

pts.k: Anonymous commenters predict that prompt-count incentives may generate unproductive use rather than useful legal work.
pts.d: Commenter 1, a self-described Shoosmiths associate, satirically suggests earning the bonus through recipe prompts. Commenter 2 characterises the scheme as marketing for efficiency and value and predicts associates will enter irrelevant prompts to protect their bonus prospects. Commenter 3 proposes an automated counting prompt. These are criticisms and hypothetical gaming scenarios, not evidence that gaming occurred. Commenter 7 tentatively disputes the technical feasibility of commenter 3's suggestion.

pts.k: Anonymous commenters question tool choice, while a self-described partner predicts productivity and career advantages for lawyers who learn to use AI.
pts.d: Commenter 4 suggests that Harvey or an internally developed tool might build more legal-specific capability than generalist Copilot. Commenter 5 expresses dissatisfaction with the platform without supplying performance evidence. Commenter 6, a self-described partner, predicts that AI-skilled colleagues will become more productive by reducing mundane administrative work and warns that resistance could jeopardise continued employment. This warning is the commenter's view, not Shoosmiths' stated employment policy.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of a reported firm announcement, examples of other organisations' policies, references to earlier reporting, and anonymous opinions.
pts.d: The incentive scheme, training partnership and internal roles are reported organisational actions. Time savings, non-replacement and sustainability benefits are attributed to Shoosmiths rather than supported by measured outcomes. The four-prompts-per-day estimate is the firm's calculation, with no workforce denominator or calculation period supplied. The article references prior adoption and attitude percentages but provides no sample sizes or methods in the supplied text. Commenters provide no benchmarks, time studies or documented cases supporting their productivity, tool-quality or gaming claims; their professional identities are self-described.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The scheme is reported in April 2025 and is conditional on reaching a collective usage threshold; most predicted benefits have no specified deadline.
pts.d: The article is dated 2 April 2025. The additional bonus depends on one million Copilot prompts, but the supplied text gives no explicit target deadline. Time savings and non-replacement are prospective statements without a defined horizon. Net zero is explicitly targeted for 2040. The earlier lawyer-attitude and adoption reporting relates to 2024. Comments run from 2 April to 11 May 2025; their later capture date is not the date of the claims. Commenter 6's productivity prediction depends on colleagues learning to use AI, and commenter 7 qualifies the technical objection with uncertainty.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are Shoosmiths employees and clients, with broader implications reported for other firms and legal applicants.
pts.d: Lawyers and support staff are encouraged to incorporate AI into daily work. All staff except partners and business services directors are eligible to benefit from the additional collective bonus; the excluded groups are still encouraged to use AI. Clients are the intended beneficiaries of more human-focused lawyer time. New innovation and data roles support adoption. Commenters identify potential effects on associates' incentives, staff capability and the career prospects of employees who resist adoption. Other reported policies affect lawyers at adopting or restricting firms and applicants for training contracts or pupillage.
